transient

/TRAN-shuhnt/ - rhymes with ancient · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Transient means lasting or staying only a short time.

The hostel's transient guests leave notes in the kitchen — half thanks, half directions — signed with first names only.

Worked Example

The clinic's discharge sheet divides symptoms into two columns. Dizziness on standing, it says, is transient: expect it, sit down, let it pass — it visits and moves on like weather. Numbness that stays past an hour belongs in the other column, the one printed with a phone number.

Transient is the working word because it means lasting or staying only a short time — the emphasis falls on the leaving. It promises nothing about how the stay ends or what it meant, only that it will be brief. That neutrality is why nurses, physicists, and innkeepers all reach for the same adjective.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

passing: Passing marks the moment of going by: a passing shower, a passing glance — here and gone almost at once. It is briefer and more of-the-moment than transient, which can cover weeks or a season: short in the life of the thing, but long enough to live in.

temporary: Temporary means in place for a limited time by design — the end is planned from the start, written into the contract or posted on the sign. Transient things leave of their own accord: guests, moods, symptoms, with no clause deciding when. Temporary is scheduled; transient simply passes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

permanent: settled in place for good

rooted: fixed where it belongs, at home

Where it sits · how much of a home base remains — visiting → transient → rootless

visiting vs. transient: Visiting is the mildest rung — a visiting scholar has a return ticket and a home campus waiting; a transient guest checks out with no promise of coming back.

rootless vs. transient: Rootless goes further than transient: a transient crew stays briefly and moves on to the next stop, while a rootless one belongs nowhere at all, with no base to go back to.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — trans-

Prefix — trans-: across

Root — i-

Root — i-: to go (Latin ire)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: -ing; in the act of

Put it together

Put it together: Trans- (across) + i- (to go) + -ent (-ing) = going across. The root is Latin ire, to go, shrunk to a single letter — the whole word pictures someone passing through your field of view on the way to somewhere else. A transient thing is caught in transit: here, briefly, and bound elsewhere.

Use the root in a new word: transit

Use the root in a new word: transit: Her luggage spent longer in transit than she spent at the conference.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / clinical

Transient is the level-headed word for what stays briefly — guests, symptoms, moods, populations — equally at home on a chart and in a poem. Its unit-mate evanescent is the rapturous one: an evanescent thing dissolves even as you watch. Say transient when the point is a short stay; say evanescent when the point is the vanishing itself.
